summary: St. Paul Island South Point light, Cabot Strait: lit from 1839, its 1915 cast-iron tower now stands at a Dingwall museum on Cape Breton; the island lights were discontinued in 2015.

light.characteristic: Group of four flashes every 12 s (1916 light, per Lighthouse Friends)

structures.note: Parks Canada: 27 ft (8.2 m) from base to vane; 36 curved panels bolted together. Stood at the island's southwest point 1915-1964, at the Dartmouth Coast Guard base 1964-2011, and in front of the Dingwall museum since 2011.

access.note: Museum grounds at 575 Dingwall Road, Dingwall, open; tower closed (Lighthouse Friends).

facts.agency: St. Paul Island Historical Society (owns the tower, per Lighthouse Friends); Canadian Coast Guard (the station to 2015)

events.note: First lighthouses, one at each end of the island, completed (Parks Canada). Lighthouse Friends: wooden octagonal towers, 40 ft, SW revolving white light
Fog bell in use in thick weather at the southwest light; a cannon was added a few years later

Steamer Turret Bay ran on the rocks near St. Paul Island in May 1904 and sank; the report credits 'the men at the station' with rescuing eight (station not named); the inquiry gives a loss of thirteen lives
Rescue of the survivors of the Turret Bay, 20 May 1904; Roderick McLeod, 'keeper of the light on South West Point', and son Abraham named in the 1906 reward list for it
Original wooden octagonal tower destroyed by fire: 17 Nov 1914 (Lighthouse Friends); December 1914 (Parks Canada)
Cast-iron tower designed by Dominion Lighthouse Depot staff, fabricated at Prescott, Ont.; completed December 1915
Cast-iron tower first lit early in 1916 (Parks Canada); Lighthouse Friends gives 1916 as the completion of the metal tower
Round fibreglass tower replaces the cast-iron tower and the station is automated (Lighthouse Friends)
Cast-iron tower moved to the Canadian Coast Guard base at Dartmouth, where it was displayed with a Fresnel lens in its lantern room
Tower disassembled March 2011, painted April, trucked to Dingwall in May; lantern room set on a concrete base at the St. Paul Island Museum in August 2011
Heritage Lighthouse statement of significance 2011-LR-043, dated August 2012
Both the northeast and southwest lights on the island discontinued (Lighthouse Friends; Rowlett gives the light inactive since 2015)

corrections.why: Parks Canada says the first lighthouses on the island were completed in 1839. The 1831 date in the record is the year the province placed a shelter house on the island (Lighthouse Friends), which Rowlett calls the station's establishment.
Parks Canada gives the year of construction as 1915 and says the tower was first lit early in 1916.
Lighthouse Friends says the grounds are open and the tower is closed.

corrections.proposed: St. Paul Island Historical Society (tower, at Dingwall)
corrections.why: The tower is no longer a federal aid to navigation; Lighthouse Friends says the St. Paul Island Historical Society owns it at Dingwall.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Rowlett gives 1831 as the station's establishment. Parks Canada says the first lighthouses were completed in 1839, and Lighthouse Friends gives 1839 for the towers and 1831 for a shelter house. The story uses 1839 for the light and says where 1831 comes from.
Parks Canada gives 1915 as the year of construction and says it was first lit early in 1916. The record's 1916 and Rowlett's 1916 fire date both mismatch; the story gives 1915 and early 1916.

Lighthouse Friends dates the fire 17 November 1914; Parks Canada says December 1914; Rowlett says the wood tower burned in 1916. The story gives Parks' and Lighthouse Friends' dates and notes they differ.

notes_for_editor: Location: the record's position (46.90073, -60.461111) is the St. Paul Island Museum at 575 Dingwall Road in Dingwall, where the tower has stood since 2011 (Lighthouse Friends gives exactly these coordinates). It is not the island site. No position for the island's southwest point was in the sources read, so no correction value is proposed. A human should supply one. Keepers: the 1906 reward list names Roderick McLeod, 'keeper of the light on South West Point', and his son Abraham against the rescue of the Turret Bay survivors. Lighthouse Friends' list has John McKenzie there for 1904-1910 and no McLeod. Page image checked 2026-10-27 (archive.org/details/1906v40i9p21_0345/page/n349, printed p. 268): the McLeod row is on the same line as the Turret Bay service, dated May 20, 1904, so the earlier note that the columns were unclear is resolved. The two sources still disagree on who kept the light in May 1904. The Marine keeper table for 1915 (scan p. 78, printed p. 71) lists 'St. Paul island, N.' and 'St. Paul island, S', but the names column could not be aligned by position, so no keeper row comes from the Marine tables. The Turret Bay life-boat passage is printed p. 8 (scan p. 21), checked in the page image on 2026-10-27; the footnote was corrected from p. 3. The wreck inquiry is printed p. 107 (scan p. 120), from the OCR and its page header; its page image was not opened. Fire date: 17 Nov 1914 (Lighthouse Friends), December 1914 (Parks), 1916 (Rowlett). Rowlett also calls the replacement a steel tower moved to Dartmouth and then Dingwall, and says the island light was removed. Lighthouse Friends says a fibreglass tower replaced the cast-iron one in 1964. The current island structure is not established. The Parks DFHD web page (id 14574) did not render; the statement was read from the Parks PDF. The statement of significance gives the distance as 18 nautical miles; Lighthouse Friends gives no distance. The 1831 shelter house is Lighthouse Friends' account only. Wikipedia was not used.
